title: The -ra Form in Place of the Conditional

sections.title: What quisiera really is
sections.content: You know *¿Podría traerme la cuenta?* and *Me gustaría…* from A2 Unit 26, where the conditional softens a request, and you know *quisiera* from B1 Unit 35 as a form of the imperfect subjunctive. *Quisiera* "I would like" is that *-ra* form doing the work of a conditional, so it is not a separate tense. Spanish allows this with three verbs: *querer*, *poder* and *deber*. The meaning is the same as *querría*, *podría* and *debería*, and the *-ra* form sounds a little more formal or more polished. The conditional is still the normal form in every register, and *quisiera* is by far the commonest of the three.

sections.title: Three verbs, two forms
rows: I would like (to), I would want

items.spanish: Si pudiera elegir, quisiera vivir cerca del mar.
items.english: If I could choose, I would like to live near the sea.
"Will Marta come to the party?" "She might."

items.spanish: Ana trabaja demasiado y debiera descansar un poco.
items.english: Ana works too much and should rest a little.

items.spanish: Quisiéramos reservar una mesa para cuatro personas.
items.english: We would like to book a table for four.

sections.content: Keep to these three verbs, and to the *-ra* form: *quisiese* does not replace the conditional in this way. For every other verb the conditional is the normal result clause: say *Si tuviera tiempo, viajaría*, not *Si tuviera tiempo, viajara*. Older literary texts sometimes use *-ra* there, so you may recognise it, but do not copy it.
